body: Eating less red meat is one of the most effective ways to reduce the environmental impact of your diet.
Reducing beef consumption can help lower pressure on forests and natural habitats.
Diets with less meat generally produce fewer greenhouse gas emissions.
Sustainable diets tend to contain more plant foods and less red meat.
Producing beef requires much more land than producing plant proteins such as peas or tofu.
Eating less meat can reduce water use associated with food production.
Reducing meat consumption may help decrease the need for antibiotics in livestock farming.
source: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. (n.d)

body: Livestock production uses most agricultural land globally while supplying a much smaller share of calories and protein.
Lower demand for livestock products can help conserve biodiversity by reducing land conversion.
Replacing some meat meals with legumes can maintain protein intake while reducing environmental impacts.
Replacing part of your meat intake with legumes can reduce the climate impact of your diet.
Pulses are rich in protein, fibre, vitamins and minerals while having a low environmental footprint.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

body: Diversifying protein sources helps support both human health and environmental sustainability.
Beans, lentils, peas and chickpeas are among the most sustainable protein sources available.
Pulses generally require less water than many animal-based protein sources.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

body: Combining legumes with cereals improves the quality of plant protein.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

body: Eggs and dairy products can provide protein with a lower environmental impact than red meat.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

body: Pulses naturally improve soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, reducing the need for fertilizer.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

body: Insects are rich in nutrients and may become an important alternative protein source in future food systems.
Plant-based meat alternatives can help reduce meat consumption, but their nutritional quality varies between products.
Quinoa contains all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete plant protein.
Pulses are nutritious staple foods linked to lower risk of chronic diseases.
Alternative crops help reduce dependence on wheat, rice and maize.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

body: Millets are highly resilient crops that can grow in hot, dry conditions with little water.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

body: Millets can continue producing food under climate conditions where other crops may fail.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

body: Growing more diverse staple crops can strengthen food security and resilience to climate change.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

body: Quinoa is now cultivated in more than 70 countries, helping diversify global food production.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

body: Buckwheat is naturally gluten-free and rich in fibre, protein and antioxidants.
Amaranth contains high-quality protein, including lysine.
Ancient grains such as millet, quinoa and amaranth contain beneficial antioxidant compounds.
About half of the world's habitable land is used for agriculture.
Producing plant proteins generally requires far less land than producing meat.
Choosing more plant-based meals can help free land for nature restoration.
Reducing beef consumption is one of the biggest diet changes for lowering land use.
Beef is one of the most land-intensive foods people consume.
Reducing food waste could save land larger than some countries.
Agriculture depends on healthy soils, biodiversity and ecosystem services.
Most agricultural land is used for livestock grazing or growing animal feed.
Farmland expansion is a major driver of biodiversity loss.
Around 52% of agricultural land is moderately or significantly degraded.
Around 70% of global freshwater withdrawals are used for agriculture.
Diets with fewer animal products often require less water.
Sustainable diets can reduce food-related water use by 20–50%.
Food waste also wastes enormous amounts of water used to grow food.
Water shortages could threaten food production in many regions by 2050.
Preventing food waste helps conserve freshwater resources.
The water footprint of your diet depends heavily on what you eat.
Improving water management can reduce the environmental impact of farming.
Irrigation water use has more than doubled since 1961.
Excess fertilizer use contributes to water pollution and dead zones.
Food systems generate about one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions.
Replacing some animal protein with legumes can lower dietary emissions.
Buying seasonal foods can help reduce food-related emissions.
Foods with the same calories can have very different carbon footprints.
Meat, especially beef and lamb, has a much higher carbon footprint than most plant foods.
Vegetarian diets can produce substantially fewer emissions than meat-heavy diets.
Flexitarian diets can significantly reduce climate impacts.
Food waste generates billions of tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions annually.
Protecting forests prevents large carbon emissions from land conversion.
Crop rotations with legumes can reduce the carbon footprint of crop production.
Global food transport generates about 3 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions each year.
Long-distance transport often requires refrigeration, which increases the energy use and carbon footprint of food.
Choosing seasonal foods and reducing unnecessary transport can help lower the climate impact of the food system.
Nearly one-fifth of the greenhouse gas emissions from the global food system come from transporting food.
Fruit and vegetables account for around 36% of food-mile emissions worldwide.
Maintaining an unbroken cold chain is essential for preserving food quality and reducing spoilage during transport.
Transporting fruit and vegetables can generate roughly twice the greenhouse gas emissions produced during their cultivation.
Although food accounts for only about 18% of global freight transport distances, it produces around 27% of freight-related emissions.
Around 526 million tonnes of food are lost or wasted each year because of inadequate refrigeration and cooling systems.
Improving cold-chain infrastructure can reduce food losses, improve food security, and reduce environmental impacts.
Food processing can improve food safety and extend shelf life.
Processing can help reduce food waste by preserving food for longer.
Ultra-processed foods are often higher in sugar, salt and saturated fat.
Different processing methods use very different amounts of energy.
Frozen foods can require substantial energy for storage.
Processing, packaging and transport all contribute to food-system impacts.
Not all processed foods have high environmental impacts.
Food processing can improve storage and transport efficiency.
The sustainability of processed foods depends on production technology.
Looking at the full food life cycle gives a better sustainability picture than focusing only on processing.
Short supply chains can support local economies and resilience.
Seasonal local food may reduce storage and transport requirements.
Country of origin alone cannot determine whether a food is sustainable.
Food origin can provide useful information about traceability and sustainability.
Global food trade has increased dramatically over recent decades.
Many European food systems depend on imported feed and commodities.
Consumers often associate origin labels with quality and safety.
Local food is not always the most sustainable option.
How food is produced often matters more than the distance it travels.
Air-freighted food can have a much larger carbon footprint than sea-freighted food.
Organic farms support higher biodiversity than conventional farms.
Climate-smart agriculture aims to improve resilience while reducing emissions.
Sustainable farming balances productivity with environmental protection.
Flower strips and pollinator habitats can support biodiversity on farms.
Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.
Crop diversification helps farms resist pests and diseases.
Agroforestry combines trees with crops or livestock on the same land.
Integrated Pest Management reduces reliance on chemical pesticides.
Precision agriculture can reduce fertilizer use and emissions.
Conservation agriculture reduces soil disturbance and protects soil health.
Diversifying crops and breeds can increase food-system resilience.
Alternative proteins may reduce reliance on conventional livestock production.
Sustainable breeding should be combined with broader food-system improvements.
Breeding animals for lower methane emissions can reduce livestock impacts.
Alternative aquaculture feeds can reduce pressure on wild fish stocks.
Genetic improvement can help crops cope with new environmental challenges.
Improving animal productivity can reduce resource use per kilogram of meat.
Genome editing may help develop crops that are more resilient to climate stress.
Selective breeding can improve feed efficiency in livestock.
Hydroponic and aquaponic systems can use far less water than conventional farming.
Agriculture accounts for most child labour cases worldwide.
Fairtrade aims to improve incomes and working conditions for farmers.
Fair trade promotes transparency and fair pricing across supply chains.
Safe and decent working conditions are a key part of sustainable food systems.
Food-system sustainability includes social and labour conditions.
Many food-system workers remain vulnerable to exploitation.
Consumers increasingly value ethical and fair food production.
Women play a critical role in food production but often have less access to resources.
Smallholder farmers produce a large share of the world's food.
Sustainable food systems should be environmentally sound and socially just.
Food packaging protects products from contamination, moisture, oxygen and physical damage, helping maintain food safety and quality.
Plastic packaging can reduce food spoilage because it is lightweight, durable and effective at protecting perishable foods.
The most sustainable packaging balances material efficiency, recyclability, product protection and food-waste prevention.
The environmental impact of producing food is often much greater than the impact of the packaging used to protect it.
Well-designed packaging can reduce food waste by extending shelf life and preventing spoilage during transport, storage and home use.
There is no single “most sustainable” packaging material; environmental performance depends on the entire product life cycle.
Edible packaging can help reduce reliance on fossil-based plastics by replacing conventional packaging materials with biodegradable alternatives.
Edible coatings can extend the shelf life of fruits and vegetables by reducing moisture loss and slowing respiration.
Smart packaging can monitor temperature, freshness and product condition, helping reduce food losses across the supply chain.
Active packaging can interact with food by absorbing oxygen or moisture, helping products stay fresh for longer.
Reusable packaging only becomes environmentally beneficial after it has been reused enough times.
Europe generates about 1.5 tonnes of single-use packaging waste every second.
Only around 40% of packaging waste in Europe is recycled.
Reusable packaging can reduce demand for virgin raw materials.
The environmental benefits of reusable packaging depend on how often it is reused.
Transport distances and cleaning processes influence the environmental impact of reusable packaging systems.
Every reusable package has a break-even point where it becomes better than single-use alternatives.
Many reuse systems in Europe already achieve return rates of 75% or higher.
Improved packaging systems can help reduce food waste by extending shelf life.
Reusable transport packaging is often designed to remain in circulation for many years.
Households generate more food waste than any other sector in the European Union.
Around one fifth of food available to consumers is wasted globally.
Shopping lists and meal planning can help reduce food waste at home.
Offering smaller portion sizes can reduce plate waste in canteens and restaurants.
Standard portion sizes often lead to unnecessary leftovers.
Many people take more food than they can eat in buffet-style dining environments.
Food waste is responsible for a significant share of food-system greenhouse gas emissions.
Wasted meat contributes disproportionately to the climate impact of food waste.
If food waste were a country, it would be one of the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitters.
Wasted food also means wasted nutrients such as protein and fibre.
Households account for more than half of food waste generated in the EU.
Proper storage helps reduce waste and keeps food safe to eat.
Perishable foods should generally not be left at room temperature for more than two hours.
Better planning and reuse of leftovers can save money and reduce environmental impacts.
Best-before dates refer to quality, while use-by dates refer to food safety.
Fruits and vegetables are the most wasted foods in Europe.
Cooling leftovers quickly helps prevent bacterial growth.
Meat and dairy may be wasted less often but have a larger environmental footprint when wasted.
Large portions of food cool faster when divided into smaller containers.
Airtight containers help keep leftovers fresh for longer.
More than half of all food waste in Europe is generated by households.
Buying more food than needed is one of the main causes of avoidable food waste at home.
Planning meals and checking cupboards before shopping can help reduce overbuying and food waste.
Freezing surplus food before it spoils can extend its shelf life and reduce waste.
Household food waste in Europe is estimated at around 69 million tonnes per year.
Confusion about “best before” and “use by” labels contributes significantly to unnecessary food waste.
Many foods remain safe to eat after their “best before” date if they have been stored correctly.
Multi-buy offers and bulk discounts can encourage consumers to purchase more food than they can use.
Fresh fruit, vegetables, dairy products and bakery items are among the foods most commonly wasted because of over-purchasing.
Keeping track of the food you throw away can help identify habits that lead to overconsumption and waste.
Portion sizes in many countries have increased substantially over recent decades.
Larger portion sizes often lead people to eat more without feeling proportionally fuller.
Reducing excessive food intake can benefit both personal health and environmental sustainability.
The environmental impact of a diet depends not only on what people eat but also on how much they eat.
Consuming excess calories contributes to higher food-system greenhouse gas emissions because more food must be produced.
Foods with high environmental footprints have an even greater impact when consumed in excess.
Choosing appropriate portion sizes can help reduce both calorie overconsumption and resource use.
Eating more food than the body needs increases demand for agricultural resources such as land, water and energy.
Overconsumption contributes to unnecessary demand for food production, transport, storage and packaging.
Sustainable diets encourage eating enough to meet nutritional needs while avoiding excessive consumption.
Protein helps build and repair muscles, tissues, enzymes and hormones.
Both plant and animal foods can provide protein.
Replacing some red meat with legumes benefits health and sustainability.
Most adults need about 0.83 g of protein per kilogram of body weight each day.
Lentils, beans, peas, nuts and seeds are excellent plant protein sources.
The overall nutritional package of a protein source matters, not just its protein content.
Eating a variety of plant proteins can provide all essential amino acids.
Quinoa is a complete plant protein containing all essential amino acids.
Protein quality depends on digestibility and amino acid composition.
Many high-income countries consume more protein than recommended.
Unsaturated fats are generally healthier than saturated fats.
WHO recommends limiting saturated fat to less than 10% of daily energy intake.
Nuts, seeds, fish and olive oil are good sources of healthy fats.
The type of fat you eat matters as much as the amount.
Trans fats increase the risk of heart disease and have no known health benefits.
Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat can improve heart health.
Fat should contribute no more than about 30% of total daily energy intake.
Low-fat processed foods may still contain high levels of sugar.
Industrially produced trans fats can be removed without affecting food availability.
Fat helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.
Sugary drinks are a major source of added sugar in many diets.
High sugar intake contributes to tooth decay.
Excess sugar intake is linked to weight gain and obesity.
WHO recommends limiting free sugars to less than 10% of daily energy intake.
Fruit contains natural sugars together with fibre and vitamins.
Reducing sugary drink consumption is an effective way to lower sugar intake.
Cooking at home makes it easier to control added sugar.
Sugar provides energy but few essential nutrients.
Reducing free sugars to below 5% may provide additional health benefits.
Reading labels can help identify foods high in added sugar.
Most people consume more than twice the recommended salt intake.
Reducing salt intake lowers the risk of heart disease and stroke.
Excess sodium intake contributes to millions of deaths worldwide.
WHO recommends consuming less than 5 grams of salt per day.
Most dietary salt comes from processed and restaurant foods.
High sodium intake increases blood pressure.
Herbs and spices can help replace salt in cooking.
Bread, processed meat and cheese are major sodium sources in Europe.
Low-sodium salt substitutes may help suitable adults reduce sodium intake.
Sea salt, Himalayan salt and table salt all contain significant sodium.
Most Europeans consume less fibre than recommended.
Whole grains, fruits, vegetables and pulses are excellent fibre sources.
Drinking enough water helps fibre work effectively.
Adults should aim for at least 25 grams of fibre per day.
Increasing fibre gradually can reduce digestive discomfort.
Whole grains provide fibre as well as important nutrients.
Fibre supports healthy digestion and bowel function.
Higher fibre intake is linked to lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
Both soluble and insoluble fibre contribute to health.
Fibre-rich foods can help people feel full for longer.
Vitamin D deficiency is common across Europe.
Vitamin C supports immunity and wound healing.
Fruits and vegetables provide important vitamins and antioxidants.
Eating a diverse diet helps reduce the risk of vitamin deficiencies.
Orange and dark-green vegetables are good sources of vitamin A precursors.
Nuts, seeds and vegetable oils are good sources of vitamin E.
Sunlight is the body’s primary source of vitamin D.
Vitamin B12 is found mainly in animal-based foods.
Vegans may need fortified foods or supplements to obtain enough B12.
Vitamin deficiencies can occur even when food is abundant.
The world already produces enough calories to feed everyone.
Nutrient-rich foods are not always the same as calorie-rich foods.
Ultra-processed foods may encourage people to consume more calories.
Foods providing the same number of calories can have very different environmental impacts.
Sustainable diets focus on food choices, not only calorie reduction.
More than half of food calories are lost between farm and plate.
Rice, wheat and maize provide nearly half of global calories.
Feeding crops to livestock results in major calorie losses.
Beef generates far more emissions per calorie than most plant foods.
Improving food-system efficiency can increase available nutrition without producing more food.
